**AI system and date:** Claude (11/5/2026)

**Our question**: Can defensive statistics in football (interceptions, fumbles forced, yards against, ect.) predict total wins in a season?

**Model:**

$$
Wins_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1(Sacks)_i + \beta_2(Yards Against)_i + \beta_3(Fumbles Forced)_i + \beta_5(Defense Interceptions)_i + \beta_6(DPD)_i + \epsilon_i
, \epsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

Fitted:

$$
\widehat{Wins_i} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1(Sacks)_i + \hat\beta_2(Yards Against)_i + \hat\beta_3(Fumbles Forced)_i + \hat\beta_5(Defense Interceptions)_i + \hat\beta_6(DPD)_i
$$

**Limitation/Opportunity:**

The limitation we wanted to address with AI is our independence problem. Our data have each NFL team repeated 22 times over 22 seasons. AI suggested a way to test if that is going to be a problem.

We also ran a Cross Validation test to test whether this new model with the combined datasets predicts outside of itself better, which it does.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#create the cv_rmse function
library(rsample)
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data, folds) {
  results <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(folds)), function(i) {
    train <- analysis(folds$splits[[i]])
    test <- assessment(folds$splits[[i]])      #maybe somebody add some comments about what is going on here
    fit <- lm(formula, data = train)
    predictions <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
    sqrt(mean((test$wins - predictions)^2))
  })
  mean(unlist(results))
}
folds <- vfold_cv(nfl_combined, v = 5, repeats = 20)

cv_results <- data.frame(
  Model = "Model 1",
  CV_RMSE = cv_rmse(formula(nfl_mod_final), nfl_combined, folds)
)
#display results
cv_results
```


:::


- **Changed** — How we adapted our data to fit our focus:

Our AI did not seem satisfied with our predictors and data in general. So we decided to combine two datasets together so we could have more predictors that could potentially help explain our response, "wins". We didn't want to leave any important defensive statistics out at the beginning. That is why the model above is slightly different from the one in our AI prompt.

- **Rejected or corrected** — AI suggestions we didn't like:

Our AI seemed very convinced that we had a serious multicollinearity problem. Looking at the VIFs, however, there wasn't as big of an issue as AI predicted. AI also suggested adding other defense variables. Unfortunately, including too many of the variables would make our analysis too complicated and unfocused.

**Connection to the final case study:** 

Our observations have each football team 23 different times—because of seasons from 2000-2022. Since our AI was so concerned about independence, it suggested that we use a **"Linear Mixed-Effects Model"**. This model will give a random intercept for each time out of a normal distribution. AI says this model will mitigate the risk of non-independence between our observations. This extension will appear on our final page where we check the "LINE" assumptions since it will help us verify the independence assumption.

According to our AI, having a 0.8313 team variance and a 5.5012 residual variance, we can compute: ICC = 0.8313 / (0.8313 + 5.5012) ≈ 0.13. This means that about 13% of the leftover variation in wins (after accounting for the defensive stats) is stable differences between teams. AI tells us that the other 87% is season-to-season noise.

**Comparison** — We just saw that the independence assumption is violated, but not horribly. To test how practical this difference is, AI suggested this code:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
      lmer_se = summary(mixed_mod)$coefficients[, 2])
```

Since the beta hats of both models are nearly the same, we are probably okay to just use our original model for the final project. Looking at SEEs would also be important for the final project.

2.  **2nd check** — This time we use the "Durbin-Watson Test."

For our second check of our Linear Mixed-effects Model we would like to do something called a "Durbin-Watson Test". This is a test that can also look at independence. Since we concluded that independence wasn't a big issue in part one, we want to check how accurate that claim is against another method. Here are the hypotheses of the Durbin-Watson test:

$H_0$: There is no correlation between the residuals (the residuals are independent)

$H_A$: The residuals are autocorrelated


::: {.cell}

Here we can see that we have a fairly high p-value of 0.11. That means that we don't have much evidence to conclude that there is no correlation between the residuals. But the p-value also isn't alarmingly high. This follows very closely with how things turned out using the linear mixed model. We will definitely have to look into this more and address it in the final project.

Citation: Statology. (n.d.). Durbin-Watson test in R. https://www.statology.org/durbin-watson-test-r/

One major limitation is we are not sure if our data has combined together correctly. Some of the rows are left our when we run certain tests. We will need to address this as we work on the final project.
